name: Which energy code each US state enforces for new homes: the IECC edition (or state equivalent) actually in force, with effective dates and amendments, from the state rules themselves
description: Which residential energy code is actually in force in a state, taken from the state's own rule or building-code authority, with the effective date and — where the rule states them — the state's amendments to it. Coverage is 9 states so far (California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, Washington), deliberately chosen to span the situations that break a one-size-fits-all answer, not the easy ones; the remaining states are listed as work to do in the asset's source notes rather than guessed at. What the pilot found: Georgia still runs the 2015 IECC with Georgia Supplements and Amendments even though it moved its other I-codes to the 2024 editions; Texas never adopted the IECC for homes at all, enforcing Chapter 11 of the 2015 International Residential Code since Sept. 1, 2016; New Jersey moved to the 2024 IECC on August 17, 2026, so anything still showing 2021 for New Jersey is out of date; Pennsylvania adopts the 2021 IECC but amends the residential envelope requirements in its own regulation; California, Florida and Oregon run state-written codes rather than adopting the IECC by name; and Colorado has no single statewide code, requiring local jurisdictions to adopt the state Model Low Energy and Carbon Code when they update any other building code. Answers 'which IECC edition does my state enforce?', 'what energy code applies to new residential construction in my state?', 'does my state amend the IECC or adopt it as written?', 'which states are still on the 2015 IECC?'
licence: Sources are US state government pages (public records). We take facts plus short attributed quotes linking back. Facts about code adoption are not copyrightable (Feist, 1991). The ICC codes themselves are copyrighted; we quote only the state's statement of which edition it adopts, not the code text.
